The change was swallowed whole. The error was generalising "widget frames cannot see lex-app's storage" from the cross-site case to every case; it is false when the origins match, which is the deployment we run. The rule is now act-versus- forget: every input may ACT, and only a `storage` event no widget claimed may clear the loop memory. That carries both requirements, where refusing to act carried only one - and the sticky stand-down was what actually stopped the mid-use reloads all along. | 1ah | Per-user metadata responses are briefly cacheable | 1.304-1.305 | complete | 9 | 0 | 0 | Follow-up to 1ag, from the user's network log: 171 requests for one Streamlit page, with api/model-structure fetched five to six times. Nothing was looping - each embedded lex-app frame is its own JS realm with its own query cache, so six widget blocks meant six independent runtimes each legitimately wanting the tree once, concurrently. That endpoint is also expensive to produce: it deepcopies the structure, then INSTANTIATES every model class and evaluates its list permission, per request. The browser HTTP cache is shared across same-origin frames, so "private, max-age=30" collapses N fetches to one with no client-side coordination and no shared-state machinery. private is load-bearing rather than tidy: the tree is pruned to the requesting user's permissions, so a shared cache serving it onward would disclose which models another user can see - a confidentiality bug, not a performance one, which is why 1.304 asserts it directly. Vary is extended rather than overwritten because DRF sets it for content negotiation and clobbering it misbehaves only under a cache. The window is a staleness budget for permission changes, so LEX_METADATA_CACHE_SECONDS=0 disables it outright; 1.305 pins that 0 means no-store rather than falling back to the default, and that a blank or malformed value cannot take the endpoint down. Also applied to model-styling, the same class of per-user metadata. |
| 1ai | Component frames load without being scrolled to | 1.306-1.308 | complete | 6 | 0 | 0 | User report - "the components trigger when I scroll to them". The cause is in Streamlit 1.58, not in the widgets: ComponentInstance renders every custom component's frame as styled('iframe')(({componentReady}) => ({display: componentReady ? 'initial' : 'none'})), so the frame is display:none until the code INSIDE it calls setComponentReady() - which it can only do once loaded. Browsers deprioritise hidden frames and commonly defer off-screen ones outright, so nothing fetches until scrolling changes visibility; Streamlit's skeleton placeholder is what was on screen. loading="eager" on our inner iframe cannot reach this, because that frame lives INSIDE the hidden one. Fix holds the frame open across its load - display:block, height:0, rendered but occupying nothing - and releases it the moment Streamlit writes a height, which only happens after ready. Deliberately inline and NOT !important: inline already beats the emotion class, and staying beatable is what lets Streamlit take the element back. 1.307 covers the part that makes this safe rather than merely effective - all three exits (ready, timeout, detached) go through one release path, because a frame left holding our styles would be permanently zero-height AFTER loading, i.e. an invisible widget instead of a slow one. Behaviour verified against DOM doubles (7 cases: nudge, leave-visible-alone, release-on-ready, release-on-timeout, release-on-detach, pick up frames from a later rerun, install once) - no JS runner in this repo, so that harness is not in CI. 1.308 fixes what the first version missed: "some iframes load when we scroll to them". Partial success is the shape of a race, not a wrong mechanism. Streamlit flips a component frame between hidden and shown by swapping the emotion CLASS, an attribute change rather than a DOM insertion, and the observer watched childList only - so a frame that existed but was not yet display:none when the first sweep ran was checked once, skipped, and never looked at again. Now observes attributes with a class/style filter (every attribute would fire on each height write Streamlit makes as components report in), plus a bounded backstop sweep for orderings not yet thought of - bounded because an unbounded timer on a dashboard left open all day is a worse and quieter bug than the one it fixes. Harness after the fix: 6/6, including the exact regression (a frame hidden AFTER the first sweep) driven through an attribute mutation with no insertion. |

Reserving the header and nav with `min-height: calc(100vh - 9rem)` is right for exactly one app - the nav's height is however many pages the author declared, so a smaller nav leaves the block floating mid-panel and a larger one grows a scrollbar in a sidebar with no reason to scroll. `min-height: 100%` on a flex column asks for the same thing knowing nothing, and grows instead of clipping. Its third half comes from READING Streamlit 1.58's styles rather than assuming them. stSidebarContent is `position: relative; height: 100%; overflow: auto` - a scroll container, and not a flex container until this CSS makes it one. Its header carries `height: theme.sizes.headerHeight`, which is a fixed height on a block and merely a starting point on a flex item: the default flex-shrink:1 would have handed the column permission to squash the logo on a short sidebar, and the navigation below it is the author's and no more ours to compress. Both are held at `flex: 0 0 auto`. The account block is the only thing that flexes and may only GROW (`1 0 auto`) - letting it shrink would squeeze the way out of the app on exactly the sidebar that is already too full, while the real scroll container sits one level up and would have handled it. 1.314 is the batch's first finding from RUNNING the component rather than reasoning about it, and it had been shipping broken. st.markdown(unsafe_allow_html=True) parses MARKDOWN first, and markdown has opinions about whitespace that HTML does not: a blank line ends an HTML block and a four-space indent is a code block. The pretty-printed markup satisfied both - so whenever the optional subtitle was omitted, its placeholder left a whitespace-only line, markdown closed the HTML block there and rendered the following indented `</div>` as literal text in a code box, in the sidebar, to the user. Invisible in every screenshot taken until then because every account anyone had looked at HAD an email for the subtitle. Both builders now emit a single line, joined with a SPACE rather than welded - HTML attributes are whitespace-separated, so joining with nothing turns `target="_top"` and `style="..."` into one unparseable attribute, which is the bug the obvious fix would have introduced. The scenario asserts no builder emits a newline at all, removing the class rather than the instance. One test-authoring fix rides along, because the same mistake was made three times in this cluster: assertions that forbid a property were tripping on COMMENTS explaining why that property was rejected. _rules_only() strips comments before asserting, so documenting a rejected approach no longer fails the test that rejects it. 1.309 covers the genuine hazard rather than the styling: the display name arrives from the identity provider and is rendered through unsafe_allow_html, so a hostile preferred_username would execute in the session of whoever opened the dashboard. Name, subtitle and the sign-out href are all escaped. Colours are derived from the vendored lex_tokens (NAVY, TEAL) rather than retyped, so the sidebar cannot drift from the product it imitates - silently, in the one place a user sees both side by side. 1.311 swaps the text wordmark for lex-app's REAL logo - the same dark-lex-logo.svg its sidenav imports, white wordmark on teal, which is what a navy surface needs. Vendored into lex/assets/ (already declared package data) rather than referenced from the frontend build, whose filenames carry content hashes and change on every rebuild - a reference would break at the next deploy and show a broken image in the one place branding matters. Placed by st.logo rather than by us. The first attempt hand-placed an <img> in the sidebar's USER CONTENT and the user reported it misplaced: that area begins BELOW Streamlit's header, so the image landed under the collapse control with the header's whitespace above it, and no negative margin fixes that honestly. st.logo renders into the header slot Streamlit reserves for exactly this - top of the sidebar, on the collapse control's line, which is where lex-app puts its logo too. The scenario asserts the SLOT rather than a measurement. Guarded on the file existing, because st.logo raises on a missing path and a packaging mistake should cost the logo rather than the page. Known limit, stated: st.logo also renders in the app's upper-left when the sidebar is COLLAPSED, and that surface follows the page theme, so a white wordmark is hard to see on a light page there; choosing a variant would mean guessing a client-side value server-side, which is the trap this session already fell into. ORDERING, after the user marked it up: logo to the very top, identity and log-out to the bottom. Streamlit's sidebar is stSidebarHeader (logo + collapse) -> stSidebarNav ->  stSidebarUserContent, so st.logo already lands above even the page navigation and identity only had to move. It is now one ACCOUNT block - identity and the way out belong to each other - rendered after main(), so the app's own navigation sits above it without either side coordinating. Call order alone puts that under the nav rather than at the foot of the panel, and pinning genuinely needs a selector, so there is exactly ONE: a data-testid (Streamlit's testing surface, far more stable than a generated emotion class) that sets layout and nothing else. If it stops matching the block sits in normal flow - where it would be anyway - so the failure mode is "not pinned", not "broken". 1.310 pins both halves of that bargain, including that the rule may not touch colour, visibility or !important: a rule that did would fail invisibly and unattributably. 1.312 fixes the residual the previous scenario had only NAMED: st.logo fills two slots with different backgrounds, and both were getting the dark file. The sidebar is brand-navy in either mode so it takes the white wordmark; the app's upper-left - where the mark moves when the sidebar is COLLAPSED - follows the page theme, so it takes the navy one (#282f63) via icon_image. Reported as the collapsed logo being nearly invisible, which is exactly white on a light page. Two files rather than one adaptive SVG on purpose: an SVG can switch fills on prefers-color-scheme, but that follows the OPERATING SYSTEM while both products deliberately default to light regardless of it, so a dark-OS user on a light page would get white on white - the same class of mismatch this cluster spent 1.261-1.276 removing. The test asserts the FILLS rather than the filenames: the names differ by one word, the files by three hex values, and swapping them yields a logo invisible on exactly one surface - which no reviewer would catch and a filename assertion would happily pass. Residual, still stated: collapsed AND dark gives navy on dark; st.logo takes one image per slot and choosing would mean reading a client-side theme from Python. Sizing and alignment, after the user marked both slots up. Size is st.logo's own `size` parameter (large) rather than CSS - a native API beats a rule that has to survive Streamlit's markup. Alignment cannot be: each slot sits flush against a different edge. In the sidebar the logo was further left than the navigation it heads; in the app header, when the sidebar is COLLAPSED, it sat against the window edge while the page's own text began well inside it. Both are pure inset corrections and join the existing bottom-pin under the same layout-only limit, which the scenario now asserts across EVERY rule in the block rather than just the pin - that limit is what keeps the whole selector dependency cheap to lose. The content inset is a single named constant in rem, since an inset in px would not track text scaling and the whole point is lining up with text. Writing this scenario surfaced a real packaging bug, unrelated to the logo and older: lex.lex_app.streamlit._widget_host_component was absent from [tool.setuptools.package-data], so the widget-host shim's frontend/ would NOT ship in a wheel and lex_widgets() would fail to find its component on any non-editable install. An editable install reads the source tree, which hides it completely. Now declared, and 1.311 asserts the rule rather than the instance: every _*_component that ships a frontend/ must be declared. |
